items.title: Amortized O(1) append
items.body: Dynamic arrays like Python lists grow by allocating a larger buffer and copying when full. An individual append can be O(n), but because capacity grows geometrically, the total cost of n appends is O(n), so append is amortized O(1).

items.title: Big-O hides constants and small inputs
items.body: Big-O describes how cost grows as input size grows, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms. An O(n log n) algorithm can be slower than an O(n^2) one for small n, which is why many sort implementations switch to insertion sort for small ranges.
items.question: Think: when does an O(n) scan beat an O(1) hash lookup in practice?
items.answer: For very small collections, a linear scan over a contiguous array can win because it avoids hashing and benefits from cache locality.

items.title: Binary search that never terminates
items.question: Your binary search uses lo = mid when the target is greater, with mid = (lo + hi) / 2, and it loops forever on two elements. What is wrong?
items.answer: With lo = mid and floor division, when hi = lo + 1 mid equals lo and the range never shrinks. Pick one invariant, such as a half-open range [lo, hi), and always move past mid (lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid). Library functions like Python bisect already get these bounds right.

items.title: Dijkstra on a graph with refunds
items.question: You model trades as a graph where some edges have negative cost (refunds) and run Dijkstra. Some shortest paths come out wrong. Why, and what do you use instead?
items.answer: Dijkstra finalizes a node when it is popped from the queue, assuming no later path can be cheaper, which only holds when all edge weights are non-negative. Use Bellman-Ford, which handles negative weights and detects negative cycles, or reweight edges as in Johnson's algorithm.

items.title: Why hash functions are randomized per process
items.question: Why does Python randomize string hashing with a per-process seed by default?
items.answer: If an attacker can predict hash values, they can submit many keys that collide, degrading hash table operations from O(1) average to O(n) and a batch of inserts to O(n^2), a denial of service known as hash flooding. A secret random seed makes collisions impractical to precompute. Go maps and Rust HashMap use seeded hashing for the same reason.

items.title: Dynamic programming: reuse overlapping subproblems
items.body: Dynamic programming applies when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Solve each subproblem once and store the result, top-down with memoization or bottom-up with a table. Naive recursive Fibonacci is exponential; with memoization it is O(n).
items.question: Think: what must you define before writing any DP code?
items.answer: The state (what a subproblem is), the recurrence relating it to smaller states, and the base cases.
